job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Ivan Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior analyst at a payments company in Milan, with a business economics degree from Bologna. I write queries, build the weekly fraud report and sit in on calls with our bank clients. I share a flat in Lambrate with two roommates, and I cook for all three of us on Sundays. I use AI tools every day, mostly to write code and draft summaries, and I like the speed of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's fine, we still get a lot out of the tools we have. To friends I'd say it's a bit boring, I was hoping for more. Online I'd post about what works and what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record it means my edge stays small. I use AI every day to write queries and draft reports, and half my team does now too. If everyone catches up, being fast with tools isn't special any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building small automations at work, like the weekly fraud report that now takes me ten minutes. I'd start a side project doing monthly books for small shops with a template and a tool. And I'd save about five hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit restless. I'm doing well and I like the pace, but I'd want something that moves faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the side project money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it brings in four hundred a month, I'd put it into index funds and one trip a year to see my grandmother in Sicily. It isn't about getting rich. It's proof I can earn without a boss, which feels like insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone catches up. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. My manager Chiara says she hires for judgement, not speed. I take that seriously, so I ask to sit in on client calls, which is where judgement shows.

say: I'd say the tools we already have give us **plenty**, and post what works online.
I'd tell friends a plateau is a bit **boring**; I hoped for more.
think: My edge stays small if **everyone** uses AI as much as I do.
Being fast with tools stops being special, so I need something more.
do: Keep building small **automations**, such as the weekly fraud report.
Start a side project doing **books for small shops**.
feel: **Calm** but restless; I like the pace and want things to move faster.

fieldNote: Uses AI **every day** and counts speed as his edge, so a plateau mostly bores him.
Sees the side project as **insurance** more than extra money.
Takes his manager's line on **judgement** seriously and asks for client calls.

steps.text: Build more small automations for the weekly fraud report

Save about 500 pounds a month into index funds
Ask to join more client calls to build judgement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's rebuild the team's process around the tools and not wait. To friends I'd say unions and governments need to catch up, because many people will be pushed to change fast. Online I'd share what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job gets reshaped within two years, and I'm one of the people who reshapes it. The danger is that the company needs three analysts where it had five. I want to be one of the three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run an internal training on the tools for the finance team and take on the model-checking work. I'd sign my first five side clients. And I'd learn enough programming to build my own tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Excited, honestly, with a bit of guilt because I know not everyone's as lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of when you say not everyone is as lucky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad Marco drives a city bus, and one day the route might be automated. And my colleague Matteo doesn't use the tools and gets nervous every time a new one lands. I do his queries sometimes, which probably isn't helping him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad to talk to his union now, not later, and I'd show him how to ask an AI about his rights. He's proud but stubborn. He'd say he doesn't need a machine to tell him anything, and then use it a week later.

say: I'd say we should **rebuild our process** around the tools and not wait.
I'd tell friends unions and governments must catch up fast.
think: The company may need **three analysts** where it had five, and I mean to be one.
I'm one of the people reshaping my job.

feel: **Fairly calm** and excited, with some guilt about those less lucky.

steps.text: Offer to run an internal tools training for the finance team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need honest talks about who stays and who goes, and about retraining everyone. To friends I'd say we should push for rules and a safety net now. Online I'd go quiet and read more than I post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one scares me, because even someone who uses the tools all day is replaceable in two years. A system that can do my job is the system I've been teaching myself to operate. My edge is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, about nine hundred a month, and cut my own spending on eating out and travel. I'd push the side project towards work that needs a person in the room, like helping a shop owner with their accounts. And I'd join my dad's union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a buzz of curiosity I'd feel guilty about. It's the biggest story of my life and I'm in the middle of it, but my plan is thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years not leave time for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't leave time for a master's, or for building a business that has customers and a name. Five years would. Two years is enough to survive, not to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents have a small flat and little savings. If I lose my job I'd be the one supporting them, which I'd planned to do later. That's the part that keeps me awake, more than my own paycheck.

say: I'd ask for **honest talks** about who stays, who goes and who gets retrained.
I'd tell friends to push for **rules** and a safety net now.
think: Even someone using the tools all day is **replaceable** in two years; my edge is gone.
The system I taught myself to run is the one that replaces me.
do: Save about **£800 a month** and cut eating out and travel.
Shift the side project to work that needs a **person in the room**.
feel: **Anxious**, with a guilty buzz of curiosity, and a thin plan.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to survive, not to switch.
fieldNote: His **usual confidence** drops because his skill is the thing being replaced.
The weight is on **supporting his parents**, which he planned to do later.
Curiosity still shows through, and he feels guilty about it.

steps.text: Save 800 pounds a month and cut eating out and travel
Cut my own spending on holidays and takeaways
Move the side project towards in-person help for shop owners
Join my dad's union and go to its meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years means we should redesign our roles now, so we're not the last to move. To friends I'd say start building something of your own. Online I'd write about the skills that keep their value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I have a real window. If I use it well I can be the person who builds with the tools, not the one replaced by them. If I waste it, I'm a junior with a thin CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small tools firm on the side now and aim for ten small clients in two years. I'd move my savings into low-cost funds and maybe buy a small flat with a friend. And I'd learn the basics of how these models are trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but charged. It's like waiting for a train. You can't tell if you'll make it, but you can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can fail once. In two years one failure ends it. In five, a first company can flop and the second one can work, so I'd actually try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the side business doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take the best offer from a bigger company that still needs someone who understands both the tools and the finance. It would be a safe landing. My degree and my work history still count for something.

say: I'd say we should **redesign our roles** now, so we're not the last to move.
I'd tell friends to build **something of their own**.
think: Five years is a real **window** to be the person who builds with the tools.
If I waste it I'm a junior with a thin CV.
do: Start a small **tools firm** on the side aiming for ten clients.
Move savings into **low-cost funds** and maybe buy a flat with a friend.
Learn how the models are trained.
feel: **Uneasy but charged**, like running for a train.
S3.quote: I can fail once. In two years one failure ends it.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **fail once**, which changes how boldly he plans.
Has a **fallback** in a bigger firm that needs finance and tools skills.
Thinks about money as a springboard, not just a cushion.

steps.text: Start a small tools firm on the side with ten target clients
Move savings into low-cost index funds
Learn how the models behind our tools are trained
Take a bigger firm's offer if the side firm fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is plenty to rebuild how we work, so let's be thoughtful. To friends I'd say this is the best time to be young and curious. Online I'd be upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good. I'd be thirty-two with a decade to build something. Maybe the business I start now becomes the main thing, or maybe I do something no one has named yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep learning, save for a flat in Milan with a mortgage I could manage, and grow the side business slowly. I'd look at a part-time master's in data and economics. And I'd vote for a shorter working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited. Ten years is a lot of time to make good mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who owns it. If a few firms control the models, small businesses like mine are tenants. I'd argue for open models and rules about sharing the gains. That's the progressive in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to ask good questions, because answers will be cheap. And build things with their hands as well as their heads, since I think people will value that more, not less.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** to rebuild how we work, so let's be thoughtful.
I'd tell friends it's the best time to be **young and curious**.
think: I'd be thirty-two with a **decade to build** something, maybe a business no one has named.
do: Keep working, save for a **flat in Milan** and grow the side business slowly.
Look at a part-time **master's** in data and economics.
Vote for a shorter working week.
feel: **Calm** and excited; ten years allows plenty of good mistakes.
S4.quote: Ten years is a lot of time to make good mistakes.
fieldNote: Moves from **personal worry** to who owns the models, a political concern.

steps.text: Keep growing the side business slowly alongside my job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is enough to survive but not to switch, and my parents would depend on me. Rules that make firms share the gains would help, and a retraining fund open to everyone, not only graduates like me. Open models too, so small firms aren't tenants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know I'm lucky. I'd like to spend some of that luck on people who aren't.

headlineQuote: Learn to ask good questions, because answers will be cheap.
portrait: Ivan is a **22-year-old junior analyst** in Milan, top of his class, with no debt and family backing.
He uses AI **every day** and treats it as his edge, so he stays calm at most speeds.
He blames **concentrated ownership**, not the tools, and wants shared gains and open models.
His one fear is the **2028 picture**, where his edge vanishes and his parents would depend on him.
He plans around **side income** and index funds, and feels guilty about those less lucky.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because two years is enough to survive but not to switch.
whatWouldHelp: **Rules** that make firms share the gains.
A **retraining fund** open to everyone, plus open models so small firms aren't tenants.
